question: Estimate the number of distinct job postings published in the United States during calendar year 2026 (2026-01-01 to 2026-12-31) for new-graduate roles — summer internships plus full-time entry-level positions for new bachelor's or master's graduates with 0–1 years of experience, in professional (white-collar) occupations — whose posting text explicitly states that the employer will sponsor a work visa (for example "H-1B sponsorship available" or "visa sponsorship provided"). Count each posting once even if it appears on several job boards. Do not count postings that do not state sponsorship in their text, even if the employer has sponsored visas before or ticks a "will sponsor" box on a job platform, and do not count postings that rule sponsorship out.

target.what: Distinct U.S. job postings first published in calendar year 2026 for new-graduate roles — summer internships plus full-time entry-level positions for new bachelor's or master's graduates with 0–1 years of experience — in professional/white-collar occupations, whose posting text explicitly states tha
target.publisher: No official publisher; analyst-constructed estimate from job boards, employer career sites, administrative immigration data, and hiring surveys.
target.cadence: Annual estimate; no official recurring series.
target.caveats: Working interpretation: one count per unique employer requisition/posting after cross-board deduplication, assigned to its first publication date in 2026; roles must be U.S.-based, professional/white-collar, and either summer internship or full-time entry-level requiring 0–1 years and targeting new

candidates.hypothesis: The target can be estimated top-down as total U.S. professional white-collar unique postings first published in 2026 multiplied by the share for new bachelor's/master's 0–1 years or summer internships and by the share explicitly stating visa sponsorship. The first two factors set the at-risk universe; if professional postings or new-grad hiring rebound, the target rises. Transfer assumption: job-board experience-level and occupation tags approximate the question's role definitions.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly or quarterly U.S. unique job postings for 2025–2026 through 2026-10-28 by occupation and experience level, ideally from Indeed Hiring Lab, Lightcast, LinkUp or similar; new-grad/internship share of professional postings; definitions and deduplication method. Substitute: total online postings series plus occupation mix and entry-level shares from BLS/JOLTS and job-board reports.
search_hints: Indeed Hiring Lab US job postings 2026
Lightcast job postings data 2026 occupation experience level
new graduate job postings share professional occupations 2026

candidates.hypothesis: The target is highly sensitive to the share of new-grad professional postings whose text contains explicit sponsorship phrases. Measuring phrase prevalence on major boards for 2026 gives a direct multiplier on the at-risk universe. If sponsorship language is rare and falling, the target falls; if employers increasingly advertise sponsorship to attract international students, the target rises. Transfer assumption: sampled boards and occupations represent all U.S. new-grad professional postings after deduplication.
candidates.data_to_find: Counts and denominators for new-grad/internship professional postings with exact phrases such as 'visa sponsorship available', 'H-1B sponsorship', and 'sponsorship provided' on LinkedIn, Indeed, Handshake, Glassdoor, ZipRecruiter, and employer sites for 2025–2026; by occupation/industry; wording variants and exclusion of 'no sponsorship'. Minimum: sample counts with denominators and date windows; substitute: platform search-result counts or a longitudinal phrase-share study.
search_hints: site:linkedin.com/jobs "visa sponsorship" "new grad" 2026
"H-1B sponsorship available" entry level 2026
"visa sponsorship provided" internship 2026

candidates.hypothesis: Employers that actually sponsor H-1B visas form a constrained set; LCA and H-1B employer/occupation data identify likely sponsors and their entry-level hiring occupations. Target postings should scale with cap-subject registrations and LCA filings for entry-level wage levels, but only where employers explicitly advertise sponsorship. If administrative sponsorship volume rises in FY2026, explicit-sponsorship postings likely rise, with lag and policy effects. Transfer assumption: administrative sponsorship activity maps to employer posting behavior after adjusting for the share that advertises.
candidates.data_to_find: USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub FY2025/FY2026, DOL LCA disclosure data by employer, occupation, wage level, worksite, and period; counts of entry-level/new-grad-compatible LCAs; top sponsor lists. Minimum: employer/occupation counts for 2025 and available 2026; substitute: public top-sponsor rankings and company filings.
search_hints: USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub 2026
DOL LCA disclosure data 2025 2026 wage level occupation
top H-1B sponsors new graduate hiring 2026

candidates.hypothesis: Summing over large professional employers and known H-1B sponsors, target postings equal their 2026 new-grad/internship requisitions that explicitly state sponsorship. Employer career sites show actual requisition counts and exact text; if top sponsors expand campus hiring and advertise sponsorship, the target rises. Transfer assumption: sampled employers represent the sponsor-advertising segment after coverage adjustment.
candidates.data_to_find: For a sample or list of top H-1B sponsors and large professional employers: number of 2026 new-grad and summer-internship postings on career sites/Handshake, whether text explicitly offers sponsorship, occupation, location, and date first posted; dedupe with boards. Minimum: 20–50 employer counts or a representative sample; substitute: search-engine counts by company and phrase.

candidates.hypothesis: Earlier-year counts of the same phrase-and-role construct, if available, provide a base level and seasonality; 2026 equals the prior-year annualized count adjusted for observed 2026 YTD labor demand, sponsorship policy, and occupation mix. If 2026 YTD runs above or below comparable prior-year months, the full-year target moves in the same direction. Transfer assumption: phrase/role definition and board coverage are consistent over time.

candidates.hypothesis: New-grad and internship posting volume is constrained by employer campus hiring plans and internship capacity. If NACE or employer surveys project higher 2026 new-grad hires and internship conversion, the at-risk universe of new-grad postings rises; explicit-sponsorship share then scales the target. Transfer assumption: hiring-plan indices and internship counts map proportionally to posting counts, not one-to-one.

Minimum: one 2026 forecast plus 2025 actual; substitute: employer earnings commentary and career-fair counts.

candidates.hypothesis: Immigration-policy changes and labor-market shocks can alter both the number of new-grad roles and whether employers state sponsorship. Restrictive H-1B rules or fees may reduce explicit sponsorship language; labor shortages may increase it. The direction of the target depends on measured exposure; these shocks must adjust any historical extrapolation. Transfer assumption: announced policy changes affect 2026 postings with identifiable timing.
candidates.data_to_find: 2025–2026 H-1B rule changes, USCIS fees and lottery announcements, executive actions, major employer sponsorship-policy changes, tech layoffs or hiring freezes, and entry-level posting trends; timing and coverage. Minimum: dated policy events and any employer announcements; substitute: news/legal analyses and job-posting trend commentary.

companies stopped sponsoring H-1B 2025 2026
2026 tech layoffs entry level hiring

candidates.hypothesis: Platform counts overcount because the same requisition appears on multiple boards and under multiple locations; the target requires unique employer requisitions. Estimating cross-board overlap and board coverage converts platform phrase counts into unique postings. If overlap is high, raw counts overstate the target; if many postings are only on employer sites or niche boards, extrapolation understates. Transfer assumption: overlap and coverage ratios from sampled postings apply to the new-grad sponsorship segment.
candidates.data_to_find: Studies or scraped samples measuring duplicate/unique ratios across LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor, ZipRecruiter, Handshake, and employer sites; job-board market share; prevalence of multi-location or reposted ads for 2025–2026. Minimum: a sample of matched postings with dedupe rules; substitute: platform unique-posting definitions and cross-posting research.

assessment.note: Indeed/Hiring Lab JPI and new-postings readings show U.S. labor demand in 2026 near or slightly above pre-pandemic levels. Many are repeated vintages of the same Indeed index, so they corroborate direction but are not independent posting-count estimates.

Unemployment, hires, quits, and labor-force measures point to a softer but not collapsing 2026 labor market. They are context for the at-risk universe, not a direct count of new-grad professional postings.

LinkUp active listings are flat around 4.6–5.0 million in mid-2026, and average closed duration is about 45–51 days. These are same-source stock and duration measures; together they support converting active listings to an annual posting flow, but only under a steady-state duration assumption.

Indeed/Hiring Lab shows about 46% entry-level postings nationwide but only 4.5% entry-level in software development and 69.3% senior in software. This establishes that 'entry-level' is broad and that professional occupations vary sharply; it does not give the narrower new-bachelor's/master's 0–1 year share.

The trylitos location-screened sample directly measures posting text: only 0.1% of all sampled US postings explicitly offer sponsorship, 0.4% of screened internships do, and most postings are silent or refuse. This is much lower than Handshake's early-career platform share and is closer to the question's explicit-text requirement.

JobShifu's large snapshot independently finds 0.18% of postings explicitly state sponsorship available and 6.13% state it is unavailable, with professional functions at 0.7–1.1% (software, data, education). This supports a low single-digit-percent explicit-sponsorship share in professional roles and conflicts with a literal reading of Handshake's 2.6% platform figure.

Handshake/CNBC-derived series says full-time early-career sponsorship fell from 10.9% in 2023 to about 1.9–2.6% in 2025–2026. This is a different measurement: a large early-career platform field/filter rather than a text audit of all U.S. postings, and it may include platform 'will sponsor' indications. It is useful as an upper-range assumption source but not as a direct substitute for explicit-text prevalence.

FY2026 H-1B cap data show about 57,600 unique employers and 336,153 eligible unique beneficiaries, with 118,660 selected. These are repeated versions of the same administrative figures; they bound the sponsor-employer pool but not the number of postings that explicitly advertise sponsorship.

USCIS/LCA employer data show a large but concentrated sponsor base: 28,277 employers with at least one new H-1B approval, 61% with a single petition, 95% with ten or fewer, and 541,620 certified LCAs. This supports an administrative employer-count route, with large transfer uncertainty from filings to advertised postings.

NACE and employer surveys point to modest growth in 2026 new-grad and intern hiring, with large-company and selected-tech employer plans stronger. These are hiring plans and survey responses, not posting counts, and several are duplicate reports of the same NACE figures.

Deduplication and syndication evidence shows very high raw duplication and a material cross-board multiplier. The saved-jobs corpus gives a concrete 210,170 rows to 88,808 requisitions collapse, while other sources give 5–20 raw appearances per role. This supports using unique employer requisitions rather than board counts, but the exact multiplier for this target is still an assumption.

Gusto small-business new-grad hiring, NACE intern conversion/wages, daily internship listing counts, and tech new-grad decline evidence all describe components of the new-grad market. They are too broad or employer-specific to directly count explicit-sponsorship professional postings, but they inform the new-grad and internship share assumptions.

params.formula: (p75 * k_days_per_year / p81) * a1 * (a2 * a3 + a4 * a5)

p75.role: U.S. active job listings in August 2026 across all occupations, LinkUp 10,000

p81.role: average closed duration in days of U.S. job listings in August 2026

a1.role: assumed professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings

a2.role: assumed full-time new-grad 0–1 year share within professional postings

a3.role: assumed explicit sponsorship share among full-time new-grad professional postings

a4.role: assumed summer internship share within professional postings

a5.role: assumed explicit sponsorship share among professional summer internship postings

methods.rationale: Structural flow decomposition: active listings divided by average duration gives an annual posting flow under a steady-state assumption; occupation, new-grad/internship, and explicit-text sponsorship shares then isolate the target. The main failure modes are that LinkUp active listings may not represent first-publication flow, duration may be nonstationary, and a1–a5 are transfer assumptions because no kept point directly measures the exact professional new-grad segment.

params.formula: (p75 * k_days_per_year / p81) * a1 * (a2 + a4) * p157 * a6

p75.role: U.S. active job listings in August 2026 across all occupations, LinkUp 10,000

p81.role: average closed duration in days of U.S. job listings in August 2026

p157.role: share of postings in the 2026 JobShifu U.S. snapshot stating visa sponsorship is available

a1.role: assumed professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings

a2.role: assumed full-time new-grad 0–1 year share within professional postings

a4.role: assumed summer internship share within professional postings

a6.role: assumed relative explicit-sponsorship intensity of new-grad professional postings versus all U.S. postings

methods.rationale: Alternative sponsorship-prevalence route: start from the same annual all-posting flow as m1 but use the large JobShifu direct-text snapshot share p157, elevated by a6 for the professional new-grad segment. It shares the LinkUp denominator and some shares with m1, so code may treat it as the same route; it is included because p157 is the largest direct explicit-text sample and provides a useful check against m1's assumed a3/a5.

p259.role: unique employers submitting FY2026 H-1B cap registrations

a8.role: assumed share of FY2026 cap-registering employers with at least one qualifying explicitly sponsored new-grad/internship posting

a9.role: assumed average qualifying postings per advertising sponsor employer

methods.rationale: Administrative employer-count route: the FY2026 H-1B cap employer pool is a constrained set of likely sponsors. Multiplying by the share that advertise qualifying new-grad/internship roles and by postings per advertiser gives an independent estimate of explicit-sponsorship postings. It does not rely on the LinkUp denominator, but it requires a8–a9 because administrative filings are not postings and many cap filers never advertise sponsorship in text.

p368.role: certified H-1B Labor Condition Applications filed with U.S. DOL, FY2025

a10.role: assumed share of LCA filings for new-grad 0–1 year professional roles

a11.role: assumed ratio of distinct 2026 explicit-sponsorship new-grad professional postings to new-grad LCA filings

methods.rationale: Administrative LCA-volume route: certified LCAs measure employer sponsorship activity but not advertised postings. The two assumptions convert all-level FY2025 LCA volume into the new-grad slice and then into postings that explicitly advertise sponsorship. It is distinct from m3 because it uses filing volume rather than the cap-employer count, and it is weaker because internships and pre-LCA advertising can make the posting-to-filing ratio exceed one while continuing/experienced filings push it below one.

assumptions.name: Professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings
assumptions.rationale: Management, business, computer, engineering, legal, education, and healthcare professional occupations account for a large but not majority share of U.S. employment and online postings. The 46% entry-level share in p16 is not an occupation share; p24/p26 show professional occupations are much more senior-skewed. A 45% transfer share is central with a wide range because no kept point gives the all-posting professional mix.
assumptions.applies_when: Applied to all-occupation U.S. annual posting flow in m1 and m2.
assumptions.falsified_by: A 2026 Lightcast/Indeed occupation mix showing professional postings well outside 30–60% of all U.S. unique postings.

assumptions.name: Full-time new-grad 0–1 year share within professional postings
assumptions.rationale: The national 46% entry-level share in p16 includes many nonprofessional and non-degree roles, while p24 shows only 4.5% of software development postings are entry-level and p26 shows 69.3% senior. The target is narrower than 'entry-level': new bachelor's/master's graduates with 0–1 years. Ten percent of professional postings is central but uncertain.
assumptions.applies_when: Used in m1 and m2 to isolate full-time new-grad professional postings before applying sponsorship shares.
assumptions.falsified_by: A direct count of 2026 professional postings tagged 0–1 years or new-grad showing a share outside 5–20%.

assumptions.name: Explicit sponsorship share among full-time new-grad professional postings
assumptions.rationale: Direct text samples give 0.1% of all postings (p125), 0.18% in JobShifu (p157), 0.4% of internships (p128), and 0.7–1.1% in professional functions such as software, data, and education (p164, p167, p162). Professional new-grad roles should be above the all-posting average but below Handshake's 2.6% platform field (p169), so 1.0% is central with a wide range.
assumptions.applies_when: Applied to full-time new-grad professional postings in m1.
assumptions.falsified_by: A 2026 phrase audit of full-time new-grad professional postings yielding a share outside 0.2–3.0%.

assumptions.name: Summer internship share within professional postings
assumptions.rationale: The trylitos all-posting sample contains 984 internship postings out of 11,304 (p126/p122), about 8.7%, but that includes nonprofessional internships and is broader than summer professional internships. NACE reports modest 2026 intern hiring growth (p526) and high employer participation (p530). Three percent of professional postings is a central transfer assumption.
assumptions.applies_when: Used in m1 and m2 to add the summer internship component.
assumptions.falsified_by: A 2026 occupation-tagged internship audit showing professional summer internships far outside 1–8% of professional postings.

assumptions.name: Explicit sponsorship share among professional summer internship postings
assumptions.rationale: The screened U.S. internship sample directly finds 0.4% explicitly offering sponsorship and 17.3% refusing (p128, p127). Professional/tech internships may be somewhat above the all-internship average, but explicit internship sponsorship is still rare.
assumptions.applies_when: Applied to professional summer internship postings in m1.
assumptions.falsified_by: A 2026 professional internship text audit showing explicit sponsorship outside 0.1–1.7%.

assumptions.name: Relative explicit-sponsorship intensity of new-grad professional postings versus all U.S. postings
assumptions.rationale: JobShifu's all-posting explicit-offer share is 0.18% (p157), while its professional functions show 0.81% software, 0.7% data, and 1.11% education (p164, p167, p162), roughly four to six times the all-posting rate. New-grad professional postings may be somewhat less sponsor-friendly than experienced professional roles, so a central factor of 4 with a wide range is used rather than copying the professional-function ratios directly.
assumptions.applies_when: Used in m2 to transfer the all-posting JobShifu explicit-offer share to new-grad professional postings.
assumptions.falsified_by: A direct comparison showing new-grad professional explicit-sponsorship share is not elevated relative to all postings.

assumptions.name: Share of FY2026 H-1B cap-registering employers with at least one qualifying explicitly sponsored new-grad/internship posting
assumptions.rationale: About 57,600 unique employers submitted FY2026 cap registrations (p259), but 61% had a single new H-1B petition and 95% had ten or fewer (p323, p324), and only 0.3% of employers in the trylitos all-posting sample had any sponsorship-offering posting (p135). Cap filers are selected sponsors, so their advertising rate should be above the all-employer 0.3% but still a minority; 8% is central with a wide range.
assumptions.applies_when: Used in m3 with p259 to estimate the count of employer-advertised qualifying postings.
assumptions.falsified_by: An employer-level 2026 audit of cap filers showing the share with qualifying explicit-sponsorship new-grad postings outside 2–20%.

assumptions.name: Average qualifying postings per advertising sponsor employer
assumptions.rationale: Most cap-registering employers are small (p323, p324), but large campus recruiters post multiple internships and full-time reqs. The trylitos samples average about 3.9 internship postings per employer (p353) and about 5.7 total postings per employer (p122), so 3 qualifying sponsored new-grad/internship postings per advertising employer is central with a wide range.
assumptions.applies_when: Used in m3 to convert advertising sponsor employers into postings.
assumptions.falsified_by: An employer-level count showing the average qualifying postings per advertising sponsor outside 1–8.

assumptions.name: Share of LCA filings for new-grad 0–1 year professional roles
assumptions.rationale: The 541,620 certified LCAs in p368 cover all H-1B levels and continuing employment. Median H-1B salary is high (p369), and software developer example rows show many workers per occupation (p361/p362). The target is new bachelor's/master's 0–1 years, a small slice of LCA volume. Three percent is central with a wide range.
assumptions.applies_when: Used in m4 to isolate the new-grad share of certified LCA volume.
assumptions.falsified_by: LCA wage-level or experience-level data showing new-grad 0–1 year LCAs outside 1–8% of certified filings.

assumptions.name: Ratio of distinct 2026 explicit-sponsorship new-grad professional postings to new-grad LCA filings
assumptions.rationale: A posting can precede an LCA and may cover internships that do not immediately require H-1B, so postings could exceed filings; conversely many LCAs are for experienced or continuing workers and are never separately advertised to new grads. The ratio is therefore near one but highly uncertain.
assumptions.applies_when: Used in m4 to translate new-grad LCA volume into explicit-sponsorship postings.
assumptions.falsified_by: A linkage study showing explicit-sponsorship new-grad postings per new-grad LCA outside 0.3–2.0.

assessment.note: Broad U.S. labor-demand indicators show postings roughly at or slightly above pre-pandemic levels in 2026, with modest positive year-over-year growth and mixed hiring rates. They support a stable-to-slightly-improving posting universe but do not identify new-grad professional sponsorship postings.

LinkUp active U.S. listings are about 4.6–4.96 million in August 2026, with average closed duration rising from 45.3 to 50.5 days. Stock divided by duration gives an annualized new-posting flow; the 4.96M and 4.6M variants are close enough to support a common order of magnitude, though they may use different dedup/coverage definitions.

Indeed reports 46% of postings as entry-level nationally, but the 0–1-year experience band is much narrower in a local Lightcast-type tabulation (about 14%), and software development entry-level postings are only 4.5% while senior is 69.3%. Broad entry-level shares overstate the target's 0–1-year new-grad professional universe; a much smaller share should be used.

A September 2026 location-screened sample finds 0.1% of all U.S. postings explicitly offering sponsorship, 0.4% of internship postings offering it, 94% silent, and 5.9% refusing. This is direct text evidence but a single board mix/snapshot; it supports a low single-digit sponsorship share for the broader posting universe and a very low internship share.

A large 2026 JobShifu snapshot reports 2,673 of 1,482,236 postings stating sponsorship available (0.18%), 6.13% stating it is not available, and 93.7% silent. Function splits are 0.7–1.11% for software/data/education. This is direct explicit-language evidence but is a snapshot, not annual first-publication counts, and is not restricted to new-grad roles.

Indeed Hiring Lab reports 0.14% of all U.S. postings mentioning visa/green-card sponsorship in May 2025, down from a 0.16% peak in October 2024 and far above the 0.04% post-pandemic low. Occupation-specific rates are higher for physicians (3.2%), therapy (1%), dental (0.6%), and pharmacy (0.5%). This supports low overall explicit-sponsorship prevalence with strong occupational heterogeneity.

Handshake early-career data show full-time postings offering visa sponsorship falling from 10.9% in 2023 to 1.9% in 2025 and 2.6% in 2026. This is the closest available segment to early-career full-time roles, but it is platform-specific and the 2025/2026 values imply measurement or coverage differences that should be handled with a wide transfer range.

F1 Hire/ITFI-style studies find only about 1.6% of U.S. openings with sponsorship-friendly language and about 12% explicitly requiring citizenship/green card. The 1.6% definition is broader than explicit H-1B sponsorship and covers all experience levels, so it is a contextual upper-ish bound rather than a direct target share.

FY2026 H-1B cap data show 336,153 unique beneficiaries, 118,660 selected, a 35.3% selection rate, 343,981 registrations, and about 57,600 unique employers, compared with 423,028 beneficiaries and 52,700 employers in FY2025. Administrative sponsorship volume is large but measures registrations/beneficiaries, not job postings or explicit advertising.

USCIS/H-1B employer data show Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Google as top initial-employment sponsors, 28,277 employers approved for at least one new H-1B worker, 61% with a single petition and 95% with ten or fewer, plus 541,620 certified LCAs in FY2025. This supports an employer-count route but requires a large transfer assumption from sponsorship filings to explicitly advertised new-grad postings.

NACE and employer surveys point to modest 2026 new-grad hiring growth (spring projection +5.6%, fall median -2.4%), intern hiring +3.9%, intern conversion 63.1%, and some large employers expanding entry-level hiring. These support a stable-to-slightly-growing new-grad posting universe, but survey plans are not posting counts.

Tech-sector evidence shows large layoffs and a collapse in Tech Majors and startup new-grad hiring versus 2019 (down about 65% and 76%). This conflicts with aggregate NACE optimism and matters because tech is a major H-1B-sponsoring segment, pushing the target toward the lower end.

Multi-source dedup evidence shows the same requisition can appear 5–20 times across raw boards, naive aggregation can be 30–40% duplicates, and production dedup can remove about 95% of duplicates. The target is unique employer postings, so raw platform phrase counts must not be used without dedup/coverage adjustment.

Policy and international-pipeline evidence is restrictive: F-1 visas fell 36%, the H-1B fee regime tightened, employer H-1B filings reportedly fell, and recruiters consider offshoring. This lowers both the number of new-grad roles and employers' willingness to state sponsorship, supporting a lower 2026 target than a simple historical extrapolation would give.

Lightcast/JOLTS flow evidence indicates monthly new-vacancy flow is roughly 40–60% of the active vacancy stock, and dedup algorithms catch about 80% of duplicates. This supports using an active-stock-over-duration flow conversion rather than treating active listings as annual postings.

params.formula: (p75 * k_days_per_year / p81) * a1 * (a2 * p169 + a4 * p128)

p75.role: U.S. active job listings in August 2026 across all occupations, LinkUp 10,000 stock

p81.role: average closed duration in days of U.S. job listings in August 2026

p169.role: share of Handshake full-time early-career job postings explicitly offering visa sponsorship, 2026

p128.role: share of screened U.S. internship postings that explicitly offer visa sponsorship, September 2026

a1.role: professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings, 2026

a2.role: full-time new-grad 0–1 year share within professional postings, 2026

a4.role: summer internship share within professional postings, 2026

methods.rationale: Reuses the round-1 stock/duration flow and improves the sponsorship shares by using Handshake's 2026 early-career full-time sponsorship rate for full-time new-grad roles and the direct September 2026 internship text-screening rate for internships. Main failures: LinkUp stock may not be a pure unique-requisition stock; Handshake's full-time early-career base may not match professional new-grad postings; the 0–1-year and internship shares are broad assumptions. The formula sums full-time and internship components rather than double-counting them.

params.formula: (p75 * k_days_per_year / p81) * a1 * (a2 + a4) * p157 * a6

p75.role: U.S. active job listings in August 2026 across all occupations, LinkUp 10,000 stock

p81.role: average closed duration in days of U.S. job listings in August 2026

p157.role: share of postings in the 2026 JobShifu U.S. snapshot stating visa sponsorship is available

a1.role: professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings, 2026

a2.role: full-time new-grad 0–1 year share within professional postings, 2026

a4.role: summer internship share within professional postings, 2026

a6.role: relative explicit-sponsorship intensity of new-grad professional postings versus all U.S. postings

methods.rationale: Reuses the round-1 all-posting explicit-sponsorship route and improves it with the large 2026 JobShifu snapshot. It starts from annualized all-occupation posting flow, restricts to professional new-grad/internship roles, applies the all-posting 0.18% explicit-sponsorship rate, and adjusts by a relative-intensity factor supported by function-level rates and Handshake early-career data. Failure modes: JobShifu is a snapshot and may not represent first publications; a6 is uncertain; stock/duration is a steady-state approximation.

p259.role: unique employers submitting FY2026 H-1B cap registrations

a8.role: share of FY2026 H-1B cap-registering employers with at least one qualifying explicitly sponsored new-grad/internship posting

a9.role: average qualifying postings per advertising sponsor employer

a7.role: coverage ratio of cap-registering sponsor universe: qualifying postings by FY2026 cap-registering employers divided by all qualifying postings

methods.rationale: Reuses the round-1 administrative employer-count route and anchors it to FY2026 cap-registering employers. The coverage factor a7 expands the cap-registering segment to all qualifying explicit-sponsorship postings, repairing the audit that the cap registrants alone are only a sponsor segment. It assumes only a minority of cap registrants advertise qualifying new-grad/internship roles and that such advertisers post several requisitions. It is independent of board coverage but depends heavily on a8/a9/a7 and on registrations mapping to 2026 postings.

p368.role: certified H-1B Labor Condition Applications filed with U.S. DOL, FY2025

a10.role: share of LCA filings for new-grad 0–1 year professional roles

a11.role: ratio of distinct 2026 explicit-sponsorship new-grad professional postings to new-grad LCA filings

a5.role: coverage ratio of LCA-filing sponsor universe: qualifying postings by LCA-filing employers divided by all qualifying postings

methods.rationale: Reuses the round-1 LCA route. Certified LCAs measure actual intended H-1B employment and are large enough to constrain the sponsor universe, but they include experienced and continuing workers and do not require advertised sponsorship language. The coverage factor a5 expands the LCA-filing segment to all qualifying explicit-sponsorship postings, repairing the audit that LCA filers alone are only a sponsor segment. The two transfer factors and a5 are the main uncertainty.

p154.role: postings stating visa sponsorship is available in the 2026 JobShifu U.S. snapshot

p153.role: total U.S. postings read in the 2026 JobShifu sponsorship snapshot

p75.role: U.S. active job listings in August 2026 across all occupations, LinkUp 10,000 stock

p81.role: average closed duration in days of U.S. job listings in August 2026

a12.role: share of all explicit-sponsorship U.S. postings that are new-grad professional roles

methods.rationale: Uses the direct count of postings stating sponsorship is available in the JobShifu snapshot, scales that snapshot to the LinkUp active-listing universe, annualizes via average listing duration, and applies the share that are new-grad professional. It avoids relying on a sponsorship-share denominator and instead uses the raw explicit-sponsorship count, but it depends on the two board universes being comparable and on the share a12. The rejected a13 is renumbered a12 so the assumption id is valid.

assumptions.name: Professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings
assumptions.rationale: Management, business, science, and arts occupations are a large but minority share of all U.S. postings; broad professional/white-collar definitions typically fall in the 35–55% range. The range allows for narrower professional definitions and lower-skill posting mix.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert all-occupation posting flow into a professional/white-collar universe.
assumptions.falsified_by: Direct 2026 all-posting occupation tabulation showing professional white-collar share far outside 30–60%.

assumptions.name: Full-time new-grad 0–1 year share within professional postings
assumptions.rationale: Broad Indeed 'entry-level' is 46%, but the target requires 0–1 years and new bachelor's/master's targeting. A local tabulation finds about 14% of unique postings with minimum experience 0–1, and professional roles skew more senior; 10% is central with a wide range for definitional uncertainty.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to isolate full-time 0–1-year professional postings from all professional postings.
assumptions.falsified_by: A 2026 professional-occupation tabulation showing the 0–1-year new-grad share outside 5–20%.

assumptions.name: Summer internship share within professional postings
assumptions.rationale: A September 2026 location-screened sample has 984 internship postings out of 11,304 U.S. postings (about 8.7%); professional internships should be somewhat less common than all internships, so 6% is central with a wide range.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to isolate professional summer internships from all professional postings.
assumptions.falsified_by: A direct 2026 professional posting sample showing internship share outside 3–12%.

assumptions.name: Relative explicit-sponsorship intensity of new-grad professional postings versus all U.S. postings
assumptions.rationale: All-posting explicit sponsorship is about 0.18% in 2026, while software/data/education functions are 0.7–1.11% and physician roles 3.2%; Handshake early-career full-time is 2.6%. New-grad professional roles should be several times the all-posting rate but not uniformly 14x, so 4x is central.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to transfer the all-posting JobShifu explicit-sponsorship share to the new-grad professional segment.
assumptions.falsified_by: Direct 2026 new-grad professional text audit showing sponsorship intensity relative to all postings outside 1.5–10x.

assumptions.name: Share of FY2026 H-1B cap-registering employers with at least one qualifying explicitly sponsored new-grad/internship posting
assumptions.rationale: Most cap registrants are existing sponsors of experienced workers, staffing/consulting firms, or small employers; only a minority hire new bachelor's/master's graduates and explicitly advertise sponsorship. 61% file a single petition and 95% file ten or fewer, supporting a low share.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert unique FY2026 H-1B cap-registering employers into employers that advertise qualifying new-grad/internship roles.
assumptions.falsified_by: Employer-site audit showing a much larger or smaller share of cap registrants with explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.

assumptions.name: Average qualifying postings per advertising sponsor employer
assumptions.rationale: Large campus recruiters post multiple new-grad and internship requisitions, while the median sponsor files few petitions and may post one. A mean of about 3 with a wide range reflects this skew.
assumptions.applies_when: Used with the advertising-sponsor employer count to estimate distinct qualifying postings.
assumptions.falsified_by: A 2026 employer-level count of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings showing mean postings per advertising sponsor outside 1–8.

assumptions.name: Share of LCA filings for new-grad 0–1 year professional roles
assumptions.rationale: Most H-1B LCAs are for experienced or continuing workers; entry-level roles have low lottery selection and are a minority of filings. Three percent is central with a wide range because new-grad professional hiring is concentrated among some sponsors.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to isolate the new-grad 0–1-year portion of certified LCAs before converting to advertised postings.
assumptions.falsified_by: LCA wage-level/occupation tabulation for 2026 showing new-grad 0–1-year share outside 1–8%.

assumptions.name: Ratio of distinct 2026 explicit-sponsorship new-grad professional postings to new-grad LCA filings
assumptions.rationale: One advertised posting can lead to multiple LCAs across hires, but many LCAs are never advertised with explicit sponsorship and some postings are internships. A ratio near one with a wide range is appropriate.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert new-grad LCA volume into distinct advertised postings with explicit sponsorship language.
assumptions.falsified_by: Matched employer audit showing postings per new-grad LCA far outside 0.3–2.0.

assumptions.name: Coverage ratio of LCA-filing sponsor universe: qualifying postings by LCA-filing employers divided by all qualifying postings
assumptions.rationale: Most explicit H-1B sponsorship postings come from employers that file LCAs, but cap-exempt universities, green-card-only sponsors, and employers that never actually file still post explicit sponsorship language. A high central coverage ratio with a wide lower tail lets the LCA route represent the full target after division.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to expand the LCA-derived count to all qualifying explicit-sponsorship postings, including those from employers outside the LCA-filing universe.
assumptions.falsified_by: A matched audit showing that LCA filers account for far less than half of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.

assumptions.name: Coverage ratio of cap-registering sponsor universe: qualifying postings by FY2026 cap-registering employers divided by all qualifying postings
assumptions.rationale: Cap-registering employers are the main H-1B sponsors but exclude cap-exempt employers and employers that sponsor only green cards or never enter the lottery. The ratio is lower than for the broader LCA universe because cap registration is a narrower subset.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to expand the cap-registering-employer route to all qualifying explicit-sponsorship postings.
assumptions.falsified_by: Employer audit showing cap registrants account for far less than 40% of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.

assumptions.name: Share of all explicit-sponsorship U.S. postings that are new-grad professional roles
assumptions.rationale: Explicit sponsorship postings skew toward experienced tech, healthcare, and consulting roles, but early-career full-time sponsorship is also present (Handshake 2.6% vs all-posting 0.18%). A quarter of explicit-sponsorship postings being new-grad professional is central with a wide range.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert the annualized all-occupation explicit-sponsorship posting flow into the new-grad professional target.
assumptions.falsified_by: A direct text audit of explicit-sponsorship postings showing the new-grad professional share outside 10–50%.

params.formula: (p75 * k_days_per_year / p81) * a1 * (a2 * p169 + a4 * p128)

p75.role: U.S. active job listings in August 2026 across all occupations, LinkUp 10,000 stock

p81.role: average closed duration in days of U.S. job listings in August 2026

p169.role: share of Handshake full-time early-career job postings explicitly offering visa sponsorship, 2026

p128.role: share of screened U.S. internship postings that explicitly offer visa sponsorship, September 2026

a1.role: professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings, 2026

a2.role: full-time new-grad 0–1 year share within professional postings, 2026

a4.role: summer internship share within professional postings, 2026

previous_methods.rationale: Reuses the round-1 stock/duration flow and improves the sponsorship shares by using Handshake's 2026 early-career full-time sponsorship rate for full-time new-grad roles and the direct September 2026 internship text-screening rate for internships. Main failures: LinkUp stock may not be a pure unique-requisition stock; Handshake's full-time early-career base may not match professional new-grad postings; the 0–1-year and internship shares are broad assumptions. The formula sums full-time and internship components rather than double-counting them.

params.formula: (p75 * k_days_per_year / p81) * a1 * (a2 + a4) * p157 * a6

p75.role: U.S. active job listings in August 2026 across all occupations, LinkUp 10,000 stock

p81.role: average closed duration in days of U.S. job listings in August 2026

p157.role: share of postings in the 2026 JobShifu U.S. snapshot stating visa sponsorship is available

a1.role: professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings, 2026

a2.role: full-time new-grad 0–1 year share within professional postings, 2026

a4.role: summer internship share within professional postings, 2026

a6.role: relative explicit-sponsorship intensity of new-grad professional postings versus all U.S. postings

previous_methods.rationale: Reuses the round-1 all-posting explicit-sponsorship route and improves it with the large 2026 JobShifu snapshot. It starts from annualized all-occupation posting flow, restricts to professional new-grad/internship roles, applies the all-posting 0.18% explicit-sponsorship rate, and adjusts by a relative-intensity factor supported by function-level rates and Handshake early-career data. Failure modes: JobShifu is a snapshot and may not represent first publications; a6 is uncertain; stock/duration is a steady-state approximation.

p259.role: unique employers submitting FY2026 H-1B cap registrations

a8.role: share of FY2026 H-1B cap-registering employers with at least one qualifying explicitly sponsored new-grad/internship posting

a9.role: average qualifying postings per advertising sponsor employer

previous_methods.rationale: Reuses the round-1 administrative employer-count route and anchors it to FY2026 cap-registering employers rather than all H-1B sponsors. It assumes only a minority of cap registrants advertise qualifying new-grad/internship roles and that such advertisers post several requisitions. It is independent of board coverage but depends heavily on a8/a9 and on registrations mapping to 2026 postings.

p368.role: certified H-1B Labor Condition Applications filed with U.S. DOL, FY2025

a10.role: share of LCA filings for new-grad 0–1 year professional roles

a11.role: ratio of distinct 2026 explicit-sponsorship new-grad professional postings to new-grad LCA filings

previous_methods.rationale: Reuses the round-1 LCA route. Certified LCAs measure actual intended H-1B employment and are large enough to constrain the sponsor universe, but they include experienced and continuing workers and do not require advertised sponsorship language. The two transfer factors are the main uncertainty.

p153.role: total U.S. postings read in the 2026 JobShifu sponsorship snapshot

p81.role: average closed duration in days of U.S. job listings in August 2026

a13.role: share of all explicit-sponsorship postings in the U.S. JobShifu snapshot that are new-grad professional roles

previous_methods.rationale: Uses the direct count of postings stating sponsorship is available in the JobShifu snapshot, scales that snapshot to the LinkUp active-listing universe, annualizes via average listing duration, and applies the share that are new-grad professional. It avoids relying on a sponsorship-share denominator and instead uses the raw explicit-sponsorship count, but it depends on the two board universes being comparable and on the share a13.

previous_assumptions.name: Professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings
previous_assumptions.rationale: Management, business, science, and arts occupations are a large but minority share of all U.S. postings; broad professional/white-collar definitions typically fall in the 35–55% range. The range allows for narrower professional definitions and lower-skill posting mix.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert all-occupation posting flow into a professional/white-collar universe.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: Direct 2026 all-posting occupation tabulation showing professional white-collar share far outside 30–60%.

previous_assumptions.name: Full-time new-grad 0–1 year share within professional postings
previous_assumptions.rationale: Broad Indeed 'entry-level' is 46%, but the target requires 0–1 years and new bachelor's/master's targeting. A local tabulation finds about 14% of unique postings with minimum experience 0–1, and professional roles skew more senior; 10% is central with a wide range for definitional uncertainty.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to isolate full-time 0–1-year professional postings from all professional postings.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: A 2026 professional-occupation tabulation showing the 0–1-year new-grad share outside 5–20%.

previous_assumptions.name: Summer internship share within professional postings
previous_assumptions.rationale: A September 2026 location-screened sample has 984 internship postings out of 11,304 U.S. postings (about 8.7%); professional internships should be somewhat less common than all internships, so 6% is central with a wide range.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to isolate professional summer internships from all professional postings.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: A direct 2026 professional posting sample showing internship share outside 3–12%.

previous_assumptions.name: Relative explicit-sponsorship intensity of new-grad professional postings versus all U.S. postings
previous_assumptions.rationale: All-posting explicit sponsorship is about 0.18% in 2026, while software/data/education functions are 0.7–1.11% and physician roles 3.2%; Handshake early-career full-time is 2.6%. New-grad professional roles should be several times the all-posting rate but not uniformly 14x, so 4x is central.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to transfer the all-posting JobShifu explicit-sponsorship share to the new-grad professional segment.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: Direct 2026 new-grad professional text audit showing sponsorship intensity relative to all postings outside 1.5–10x.

previous_assumptions.name: Share of FY2026 H-1B cap-registering employers with at least one qualifying explicitly sponsored new-grad/internship posting
previous_assumptions.rationale: Most cap registrants are existing sponsors of experienced workers, staffing/consulting firms, or small employers; only a minority hire new bachelor's/master's graduates and explicitly advertise sponsorship. 61% file a single petition and 95% file ten or fewer, supporting a low share.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert unique FY2026 H-1B cap-registering employers into employers that advertise qualifying new-grad/internship roles.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: Employer-site audit showing a much larger or smaller share of cap registrants with explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.

previous_assumptions.name: Average qualifying postings per advertising sponsor employer
previous_assumptions.rationale: Large campus recruiters post multiple new-grad and internship requisitions, while the median sponsor files few petitions and may post one. A mean of about 3 with a wide range reflects this skew.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used with the advertising-sponsor employer count to estimate distinct qualifying postings.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: A 2026 employer-level count of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings showing mean postings per advertising sponsor outside 1–8.

previous_assumptions.name: Share of LCA filings for new-grad 0–1 year professional roles
previous_assumptions.rationale: Most H-1B LCAs are for experienced or continuing workers; entry-level roles have low lottery selection and are a minority of filings. Three percent is central with a wide range because new-grad professional hiring is concentrated among some sponsors.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to isolate the new-grad 0–1-year portion of certified LCAs before converting to advertised postings.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: LCA wage-level/occupation tabulation for 2026 showing new-grad 0–1-year share outside 1–8%.

previous_assumptions.name: Ratio of distinct 2026 explicit-sponsorship new-grad professional postings to new-grad LCA filings
previous_assumptions.rationale: One advertised posting can lead to multiple LCAs across hires, but many LCAs are never advertised with explicit sponsorship and some postings are internships. A ratio near one with a wide range is appropriate.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert new-grad LCA volume into distinct advertised postings with explicit sponsorship language.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: Matched employer audit showing postings per new-grad LCA far outside 0.3–2.0.

previous_assumptions.name: Share of all explicit-sponsorship postings that are new-grad professional
previous_assumptions.rationale: Explicit sponsorship postings skew toward experienced tech, healthcare, and consulting roles, but early-career full-time sponsorship is also present (Handshake 2.6% vs all-posting 0.18%). A quarter of explicit-sponsorship postings being new-grad professional is central with a wide range.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert the annualized all-occupation explicit-sponsorship posting flow into the new-grad professional target.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: A direct text audit of explicit-sponsorship postings showing the new-grad professional share outside 10–50%.

previous_assumptions.name: Relative explicit-sponsorship intensity of new-grad professional postings versus all U.S. postings
previous_assumptions.rationale: All-posting explicit sponsorship is about 0.18% in 2026, while software/data/education functions are 0.7–1.11% and physician roles 3.2%; Handshake early-career full-time is 2.6%. New-grad professional roles should be several times the all-posting rate but not uniformly 14x, so 4x is central.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to transfer the all-posting JobShifu explicit-sponsorship share to the new-grad professional segment.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: Direct 2026 new-grad professional text audit showing sponsorship intensity relative to all postings outside 1.5–10x.

previous_assumptions.name: Share of FY2026 H-1B cap-registering employers with at least one qualifying explicitly sponsored new-grad/internship posting
previous_assumptions.rationale: Most cap registrants are existing sponsors of experienced workers, staffing/consulting firms, or small employers; only a minority hire new bachelor's/master's graduates and explicitly advertise sponsorship. 61% file a single petition and 95% file ten or fewer, supporting a low share.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert unique FY2026 H-1B cap-registering employers into employers that advertise qualifying new-grad/internship roles.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: Employer-site audit showing a much larger or smaller share of cap registrants with explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.

previous_assumptions.name: Average qualifying postings per advertising sponsor employer
previous_assumptions.rationale: Large campus recruiters post multiple new-grad and internship requisitions, while the median sponsor files few petitions and may post one. A mean of about 3 with a wide range reflects this skew.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used with the advertising-sponsor employer count to estimate distinct qualifying postings.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: A 2026 employer-level count of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings showing mean postings per advertising sponsor outside 1–8.

previous_assumptions.name: Share of LCA filings for new-grad 0–1 year professional roles
previous_assumptions.rationale: Most H-1B LCAs are for experienced or continuing workers; entry-level roles have low lottery selection and are a minority of filings. Three percent is central with a wide range because new-grad professional hiring is concentrated among some sponsors.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to isolate the new-grad 0–1-year portion of certified LCAs before converting to advertised postings.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: LCA wage-level/occupation tabulation for 2026 showing new-grad 0–1-year share outside 1–8%.

previous_assumptions.name: Ratio of distinct 2026 explicit-sponsorship new-grad professional postings to new-grad LCA filings
previous_assumptions.rationale: One advertised posting can lead to multiple LCAs across hires, but many LCAs are never advertised with explicit sponsorship and some postings are internships. A ratio near one with a wide range is appropriate.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert new-grad LCA volume into distinct advertised postings with explicit sponsorship language.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: Matched employer audit showing postings per new-grad LCA far outside 0.3–2.0.

previous_assumptions.name: Share of all explicit-sponsorship postings that are new-grad professional
previous_assumptions.rationale: Explicit sponsorship postings skew toward experienced tech, healthcare, and consulting roles, but early-career full-time sponsorship is also present (Handshake 2.6% vs all-posting 0.18%). A quarter of explicit-sponsorship postings being new-grad professional is central with a wide range.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert the annualized all-occupation explicit-sponsorship posting flow into the new-grad professional target.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: A direct text audit of explicit-sponsorship postings showing the new-grad professional share outside 10–50%.

kept.name: Professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings
kept.rationale: Management, business, science, and arts occupations are a large but minority share of all U.S. postings; broad professional/white-collar definitions typically fall in the 35–55% range. The range allows for narrower professional definitions and lower-skill posting mix.
kept.applies_when: Used to convert all-occupation posting flow into a professional/white-collar universe.
kept.falsified_by: Direct 2026 all-posting occupation tabulation showing professional white-collar share far outside 30–60%.

kept.name: Full-time new-grad 0–1 year share within professional postings
kept.rationale: Broad Indeed 'entry-level' is 46%, but the target requires 0–1 years and new bachelor's/master's targeting. A local tabulation finds about 14% of unique postings with minimum experience 0–1, and professional roles skew more senior; 10% is central with a wide range for definitional uncertainty.
kept.applies_when: Used to isolate full-time 0–1-year professional postings from all professional postings.
kept.falsified_by: A 2026 professional-occupation tabulation showing the 0–1-year new-grad share outside 5–20%.

kept.name: Summer internship share within professional postings
kept.rationale: A September 2026 location-screened sample has 984 internship postings out of 11,304 U.S. postings (about 8.7%); professional internships should be somewhat less common than all internships, so 6% is central with a wide range.
kept.applies_when: Used to isolate professional summer internships from all professional postings.
kept.falsified_by: A direct 2026 professional posting sample showing internship share outside 3–12%.

kept.name: Relative explicit-sponsorship intensity of new-grad professional postings versus all U.S. postings
kept.rationale: All-posting explicit sponsorship is about 0.18% in 2026, while software/data/education functions are 0.7–1.11% and physician roles 3.2%; Handshake early-career full-time is 2.6%. New-grad professional roles should be several times the all-posting rate but not uniformly 14x, so 4x is central.
kept.applies_when: Used to transfer the all-posting JobShifu explicit-sponsorship share to the new-grad professional segment.
kept.falsified_by: Direct 2026 new-grad professional text audit showing sponsorship intensity relative to all postings outside 1.5–10x.

kept.name: Share of FY2026 H-1B cap-registering employers with at least one qualifying explicitly sponsored new-grad/internship posting
kept.rationale: Most cap registrants are existing sponsors of experienced workers, staffing/consulting firms, or small employers; only a minority hire new bachelor's/master's graduates and explicitly advertise sponsorship. 61% file a single petition and 95% file ten or fewer, supporting a low share.
kept.applies_when: Used to convert unique FY2026 H-1B cap-registering employers into employers that advertise qualifying new-grad/internship roles.
kept.falsified_by: Employer-site audit showing a much larger or smaller share of cap registrants with explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.

kept.name: Average qualifying postings per advertising sponsor employer
kept.rationale: Large campus recruiters post multiple new-grad and internship requisitions, while the median sponsor files few petitions and may post one. A mean of about 3 with a wide range reflects this skew.
kept.applies_when: Used with the advertising-sponsor employer count to estimate distinct qualifying postings.
kept.falsified_by: A 2026 employer-level count of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings showing mean postings per advertising sponsor outside 1–8.

kept.name: Share of LCA filings for new-grad 0–1 year professional roles
kept.rationale: Most H-1B LCAs are for experienced or continuing workers; entry-level roles have low lottery selection and are a minority of filings. Three percent is central with a wide range because new-grad professional hiring is concentrated among some sponsors.
kept.applies_when: Used to isolate the new-grad 0–1-year portion of certified LCAs before converting to advertised postings.
kept.falsified_by: LCA wage-level/occupation tabulation for 2026 showing new-grad 0–1-year share outside 1–8%.

kept.name: Ratio of distinct 2026 explicit-sponsorship new-grad professional postings to new-grad LCA filings
kept.rationale: One advertised posting can lead to multiple LCAs across hires, but many LCAs are never advertised with explicit sponsorship and some postings are internships. A ratio near one with a wide range is appropriate.
kept.applies_when: Used to convert new-grad LCA volume into distinct advertised postings with explicit sponsorship language.
kept.falsified_by: Matched employer audit showing postings per new-grad LCA far outside 0.3–2.0.

kept.name: Coverage ratio of LCA-filing sponsor universe: qualifying postings by LCA-filing employers divided by all qualifying postings
kept.rationale: Most explicit H-1B sponsorship postings come from employers that file LCAs, but cap-exempt universities, green-card-only sponsors, and employers that never actually file still post explicit sponsorship language. A high central coverage ratio with a wide lower tail lets the LCA route represent the fu
kept.applies_when: Used to expand the LCA-derived count to all qualifying explicit-sponsorship postings, including those from employers outside the LCA-filing universe.
kept.falsified_by: A matched audit showing that LCA filers account for far less than half of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.

kept.name: Coverage ratio of cap-registering sponsor universe: qualifying postings by FY2026 cap-registering employers divided by all qualifying postings
kept.rationale: Cap-registering employers are the main H-1B sponsors but exclude cap-exempt employers and employers that sponsor only green cards or never enter the lottery. The ratio is lower than for the broader LCA universe because cap registration is a narrower subset.
kept.applies_when: Used to expand the cap-registering-employer route to all qualifying explicit-sponsorship postings.
kept.falsified_by: Employer audit showing cap registrants account for far less than 40% of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.

kept.name: Share of all explicit-sponsorship U.S. postings that are new-grad professional roles
kept.rationale: Explicit sponsorship postings skew toward experienced tech, healthcare, and consulting roles, but early-career full-time sponsorship is also present (Handshake 2.6% vs all-posting 0.18%). A quarter of explicit-sponsorship postings being new-grad professional is central with a wide range.
kept.applies_when: Used to convert the annualized all-occupation explicit-sponsorship posting flow into the new-grad professional target.
kept.falsified_by: A direct text audit of explicit-sponsorship postings showing the new-grad professional share outside 10–50%.

final.template:
The best estimate is [[estimate]] [[unit]] ([[interval_level]] interval [[p10]] to [[p90]] [[unit]]) for distinct U.S. postings first published in 2026 for new-graduate summer internships and full-time entry-level professional roles whose text explicitly states visa sponsorship. Four routes were combined with equal weight per block: an all-posting flow route scaled by professional and new-grad shares and a sponsorship-intensity factor; a cap-registering employer route; an LCA route; and a direct JobShifu explicit-sponsorship count scaled to the LinkUp universe. Observed anchors include [[p75_value]], [[p81_value]], [[p157_value]], [[p259_value]], [[p368_value]], [[p154_value]] and [[p153_value]]. Everything else rests on analyst assumptions, notably the professional share [[a1_value]], new-grad share [[a2_value]], internship share [[a4_value]], intensity ratio [[a6_value]], coverage ratios [[a7_value]] and [[a5_value]], and new-grad share of sponsored postings [[a12_value]]. The interval is conditional on these assumptions, not a demonstrated accuracy guarantee. The biggest risk is that explicit sponsorship language is rare and inconsistently detected, so the sponsorship rate and coverage factors could be off several-fold. Better evidence would be a large, deduplicated 2026 posting sample with verified sponsorship text and new-grad classification.

Unit of the estimate: [[unit_full]].

Key assumptions (proposed by the analyst model, not observed; code samples each one between the bounds shown):
- a1 Professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings: [[a1_value]], range [[a1_low]] to [[a1_high]]; used by m1. Overturned by: Direct 2026 all-posting occupation tabulation showing professional white-collar share far outside [n]–[n].
- a2 Full-time new-grad [n]–[n] year share within professional postings: [[a2_value]], range [[a2_low]] to [[a2_high]]; used by m1. Overturned by: A 2026 professional-occupation tabulation showing the [n]–[n]-year new-grad share outside [n]–[n].
- a4 Summer internship share within professional postings: [[a4_value]], range [[a4_low]] to [[a4_high]]; used by m1. Overturned by: A direct 2026 professional posting sample showing internship share outside [n]–[n].
- a6 Relative explicit-sponsorship intensity of new-grad professional postings versus all U.S. postings: [[a6_value]] ratio, range [[a6_low]] to [[a6_high]]; used by m1. Overturned by: Direct 2026 new-grad professional text audit showing sponsorship intensity relative to all postings outside [n]–[n]x.
- a8 Share of FY[n] H-[n]B cap-registering employers with at least one qualifying explicitly sponsored new-grad/internship posting: [[a8_value]], range [[a8_low]] to [[a8_high]]; used by m2. Overturned by: Employer-site audit showing a much larger or smaller share of cap registrants with explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.
- a9 Average qualifying postings per advertising sponsor employer: [[a9_value]] posting per employer, range [[a9_low]] to [[a9_high]]; used by m2. Overturned by: A 2026 employer-level count of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings showing mean postings per advertising sponsor outside [n]–[n].
- a10 Share of LCA filings for new-grad [n]–[n] year professional roles: [[a10_value]], range [[a10_low]] to [[a10_high]]; used by m3. Overturned by: LCA wage-level/occupation tabulation for 2026 showing new-grad [n]–[n]-year share outside [n]–[n].
- a11 Ratio of distinct 2026 explicit-sponsorship new-grad professional postings to new-grad LCA filings: [[a11_value]] posting per filing, range [[a11_low]] to [[a11_high]]; used by m3. Overturned by: Matched employer audit showing postings per new-grad LCA far outside [n]–[n].
- a5 Coverage ratio of LCA-filing sponsor universe: qualifying postings by LCA-filing employers divided by all qualifying postings: [[a5_value]] ratio, range [[a5_low]] to [[a5_high]] (range widened by code); used by m3. Overturned by: A matched audit showing that LCA filers account for far less than half of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.
- a7 Coverage ratio of cap-registering sponsor universe: qualifying postings by FY[n] cap-registering employers divided by all qualifying postings: [[a7_value]] ratio, range [[a7_low]] to [[a7_high]]; used by m2. Overturned by: Employer audit showing cap registrants account for far less than [n] of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.
- a12 Share of all explicit-sponsorship U.S. postings that are new-grad professional roles: [[a12_value]] ratio, range [[a12_low]] to [[a12_high]]; used by m4. Overturned by: A direct text audit of explicit-sponsorship postings showing the new-grad professional share outside [n]–[n].

Method details (computed by code):
- m1 formula_mc: (p75 * k_days_per_year / p81) * a1 * (a2 + a4) * p157 * a6; Monte Carlo P10 to P90 [[m1_mc_p10]] to [[m1_mc_p90]]; result unit (posting/year) * 1 year converted to posting; own 80% width [[m1_width]] (Monte Carlo of the formula inputs)

final.text:
The best estimate is 15,819 posting (80% model-based interval 4,385 to 57,071 posting) for distinct U.S. postings first published in 2026 for new-graduate summer internships and full-time entry-level professional roles whose text explicitly states visa sponsorship. Four routes were combined with equal weight per block: an all-posting flow route scaled by professional and new-grad shares and a sponsorship-intensity factor; a cap-registering employer route; an LCA route; and a direct JobShifu explicit-sponsorship count scaled to the LinkUp universe. Observed anchors include 4,960,000 job posting, 50.5 day, 0.18%, 57,600 employer, 541,620 certified filing, 2,673 job posting and 1,482,236 job posting. Everything else rests on analyst assumptions, notably the professional share 45%, new-grad share 10%, internship share 6%, intensity ratio 4, coverage ratios 0.7 and 0.8, and new-grad share of sponsored postings 0.25. The interval is conditional on these assumptions, not a demonstrated accuracy guarantee. The biggest risk is that explicit sponsorship language is rare and inconsistently detected, so the sponsorship rate and coverage factors could be off several-fold. Better evidence would be a large, deduplicated 2026 posting sample with verified sponsorship text and new-grad classification.

Unit of the estimate: posting (distinct job posting; total for 2026-01-01 to 2026-12-31).

Key assumptions (proposed by the analyst model, not observed; code samples each one between the bounds shown):
- a1 Professional white-collar share of all U.S. unique postings: 45%, range 30% to 60%; used by m1. Overturned by: Direct 2026 all-posting occupation tabulation showing professional white-collar share far outside [n]–[n].
- a2 Full-time new-grad [n]–[n] year share within professional postings: 10%, range 5% to 20%; used by m1. Overturned by: A 2026 professional-occupation tabulation showing the [n]–[n]-year new-grad share outside [n]–[n].
- a4 Summer internship share within professional postings: 6%, range 3% to 12%; used by m1. Overturned by: A direct 2026 professional posting sample showing internship share outside [n]–[n].
- a6 Relative explicit-sponsorship intensity of new-grad professional postings versus all U.S. postings: 4 ratio, range 1.5 to 10; used by m1. Overturned by: Direct 2026 new-grad professional text audit showing sponsorship intensity relative to all postings outside [n]–[n]x.
- a8 Share of FY[n] H-[n]B cap-registering employers with at least one qualifying explicitly sponsored new-grad/internship posting: 6%, range 2% to 15%; used by m2. Overturned by: Employer-site audit showing a much larger or smaller share of cap registrants with explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.
- a9 Average qualifying postings per advertising sponsor employer: 3 posting per employer, range 1 to 8; used by m2. Overturned by: A 2026 employer-level count of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings showing mean postings per advertising sponsor outside [n]–[n].
- a10 Share of LCA filings for new-grad [n]–[n] year professional roles: 3%, range 1% to 8%; used by m3. Overturned by: LCA wage-level/occupation tabulation for 2026 showing new-grad [n]–[n]-year share outside [n]–[n].
- a11 Ratio of distinct 2026 explicit-sponsorship new-grad professional postings to new-grad LCA filings: 0.8 posting per filing, range 0.3 to 2; used by m3. Overturned by: Matched employer audit showing postings per new-grad LCA far outside [n]–[n].
- a5 Coverage ratio of LCA-filing sponsor universe: qualifying postings by LCA-filing employers divided by all qualifying postings: 0.8 ratio, range 0.4873 to 0.9747 (range widened by code); used by m3. Overturned by: A matched audit showing that LCA filers account for far less than half of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.
- a7 Coverage ratio of cap-registering sponsor universe: qualifying postings by FY[n] cap-registering employers divided by all qualifying postings: 0.7 ratio, range 0.4 to 0.9; used by m2. Overturned by: Employer audit showing cap registrants account for far less than [n] of explicit new-grad sponsorship postings.
- a12 Share of all explicit-sponsorship U.S. postings that are new-grad professional roles: 0.25 ratio, range 0.1 to 0.5; used by m4. Overturned by: A direct text audit of explicit-sponsorship postings showing the new-grad professional share outside [n]–[n].

Method details (computed by code):
- m1 formula_mc: (p75 * k_days_per_year / p81) * a1 * (a2 + a4) * p157 * a6; Monte Carlo P10 to P90 5,592 to 59,245; result unit (posting/year) * 1 year converted to posting; own 80% width x/÷3.26 (Monte Carlo of the formula inputs)
- m2 formula_mc: p259 * a8 * a9 / a7; Monte Carlo P10 to P90 2,097 to 42,586; result unit (0.05263157895 posting/month) * 1 year converted to posting; own 80% width x/÷4.51 (Monte Carlo of the formula inputs)
- m3 formula_mc: p368 * a10 * a11 / a5; Monte Carlo P10 to P90 3,943 to 73,945; result unit (posting/year) * 1 year converted to posting; own 80% width x/÷4.33 (Monte Carlo of the formula inputs)
- m4 formula_mc: (p154 * p75 / p153) * (k_days_per_year / p81) * a12; Monte Carlo P10 to P90 5,985 to 34,893; result unit (posting/year) * 1 year converted to posting; own 80% width x/÷2.41 (Monte Carlo of the formula inputs)
- Combination: 4 block(s), equal weight per block (methods whose inputs overlap by at least half form one block; backtest errors set widths, not weights): B1 = m1: 18,376 (width x/÷3.26, Monte Carlo of the formula inputs); B2 = m2: 9,413 (width x/÷4.51, Monte Carlo of the formula inputs); B3 = m3: 17,194 (width x/÷4.33, Monte Carlo of the formula inputs); B4 = m4: 14,554 (width x/÷2.41, Monte Carlo of the formula inputs). Estimate = the median of the blocks.
- Interval: root mean square of the block widths x/÷3.61; Birge ratio 0.27 (not above one, so no widening); final width x/÷3.61.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
